text: An atheist and a pastor walk into a bar.
The atheist orders whiskey. The pastor orders water.
The atheist laughs.
You know, for a man who believes in eternal life, you sure seem afraid to enjoy this one.
The pastor smiles.
And for a man who believes this life is all there is, you sure seem determined to forget it.
The atheist stops laughing.
After a moment, he asks the pastor a question.
If your God is so good, why does He allow innocent children to suffer?
The pastor looks down at his glass.
I don't know why every child suffers.
The atheist smirks.
That's the problem with religion. You always have an answer until the question becomes difficult.
The pastor replies.
No. The problem with some religious people is that they pretend faith means having every answer.
The atheist takes another drink.
Then tell me what faith actually is.
The pastor thinks for a moment.
Faith is not pretending the darkness doesn't exist. It's believing the darkness doesn't have the final word.
The atheist shakes his head.
That's beautiful. But beauty doesn't make something true.
The pastor nods.
You're right.
For the first time, the atheist looks surprised.
The pastor continues.
And pain doesn't make something false.
Silence settles between them.
The atheist stares into his glass.
I used to believe in God, you know.
The pastor says nothing.
I prayed every night when my daughter got sick. I begged Him. I promised Him everything. I would have given my life for hers.
His voice begins to break.
She was seven.
The pastor slowly sets down his water.
And when we buried her, everyone told me God had a plan.
The atheist looks directly at him.
Tell me, Pastor. What kind of plan requires a seven-year-old girl to die?
The pastor's eyes fill with tears.
I would never tell a grieving father that I knew why his daughter died.
Then what would you tell him?
The pastor pauses.
That when Jesus stood at the tomb of Lazarus, knowing He was about to raise him from the dead, He still wept.
The atheist looks away.
Why?
Because knowing resurrection was coming didn't make death any less heartbreaking.
Neither man speaks for several minutes.
Finally, the atheist whispers.
I don't hate God because I know He doesn't exist.
The pastor waits.
I hate the possibility that He does exist, and He watched me bury my daughter.
The pastor nods slowly.
That's a much harder question than whether God exists.
The atheist wipes his eyes.
So what am I supposed to do? Believe again?
No. I'm not going to ask you to pretend you're convinced.
Then what?
The pastor looks toward the door.

Go home. Remember your daughter. Love her without apologizing for how much it hurts. And if you ever decide to pray again, don't give God the words you think a pastor wants to hear. Give Him the ones you've been afraid to say.
The atheist looks at his empty glass.
You think God can handle my anger?
The pastor answers.
If He is God, your anger cannot destroy Him. And if He is good, your grief will not surprise Him.
The atheist stands to leave.
At the door, he turns around.
Pastor, did you ever lose someone you prayed God would save?
The pastor reaches into his wallet and pulls out a faded photograph of a young boy.
My son. He was nine.
The atheist stares at the picture.
And you still believe?
The pastor looks at the photograph for a long time.
Some days, I believe with confidence. Other days, all I can manage is to ask God why. But I learned something after burying him.
What's that?
The pastor folds the photograph carefully.
I used to think faith meant never questioning God. Now I think faith sometimes means refusing to stop talking to Him, even when all you have left are questions.
The atheist walks back to the table and sits down.
He doesn't order another whiskey.
The pastor doesn't offer another sermon.
And for the next two hours, two fathers sit together, speaking about the children they loved.
One believes in God.
The other doesn't know what he believes anymore.
But when the bartender comes to close, he notices something strange.
The atheist is praying.
And the pastor is crying.
Because sometimes the deepest conversations about God don't end with someone winning an argument.
Sometimes they end with two broken people realizing that the person across from them understands their pain.
